主要内容: The global automobile manufacturing industry is undergoing its greatest transformation ever, driven by the shift toward autonomous driving and electric-powered vehicles. This transition is forcing automakers to alter their business models and product portfolios, while also facing declining sales and increased vulnerability to external shocks. In 2019, the demand backdrop in key regions is expected to reflect declining volume and compressed margins, prompting automakers to adopt a more defensive approach since the end of the 2008-09 global financial crisis. The development of electrified vehicles is gaining momentum, particularly in Europe, where diesel engine market share is declining, and in China, where government programs are promoting a move away from fossil fuels. U.S. automakers are struggling to maintain demand as income slips, with a focus on higher-margin pickup trucks, SUVs, and crossovers. However, foreign brands are challenging this trend, leading to shorter product lifecycles and increased investment in new designs. Combined operating profit for Fiat Chrysler, Ford, and General Motors declined 11% in the trailing 12 months, resulting in a $2.8 billion shortfall compared to the same period in 2018. As competition intensifies and expenses rise for unprofitable electric drivetrains and autonomous technologies, operating profit is expected to erode further. The U.S. sales mix of these three automakers is 85% light trucks in 2019, up from 65% in 2017. Declining R&D spending is also delaying ambitious projects, with automakers cutting investments in long-term technology pursuits such as fully self-driving vehicles. Even Tesla’s R&D percentage at 7% is the lowest in its history, following explosive revenue growth from Model 3 deliveries. BMW’s 2018 R&D spending relative to net sales was the highest among global automakers at 7.1%, as German manufacturers invest in new drivetrain technology to offset declining diesel demand.
